ANNUAL MESSAGE

OF
PRESIDENT R. HAYES,
DELIVERED TO CONGRESS
DECEMBER 3, 1879.


Fellow Citizens of the Senate and House of Representatives: The members of the Forty-sixth Congress have assembled in the first regular session, under circumstances calling for mutual congratulation and grateful acknowledgment to the giver of all good, for the large and universal measure of national prosperity which we now enjoy. The most interesting events which have occurred in our public affairs since my last annual message to Congress are connected with the financial operations of the government directly affecting the business interests of the country.


I. THE RESUMPTION ACT.


I congratulate Congress on the successful execution of the resumption act at the time fixed and in the manner contemplated by Law. The notes of the United States began to be redeemed in coin since the 1st of January last, and they have been promptly redeemed on presentation and in business transactions, public and private, in all parts of the country. They are received and paid on as the equivalent of coin. The demand upon the treasury for gold and silver in exchange for United States notes has been comparatively smaller and the voluntary deposits of coin and bullion in exchange for notes have been very large. The excess of precious metals deposited or exchanged for United States notes, over the amount of United States notes redeemed, is about $40,000,900. The resumption of specie payment has been followed by a very great revival of business. With a currency equivalent in value to the money of the commercial world, we are enabled to enter upon equal competition with other nations in trade and production. The increasing foreign demand for our products has caused a large balance of trade in our favor, which has been paid in gold from the 1st of July last to November 1st to the amount of about $69,000,600.


II. REFUNDING OPERATIONS.


Since the resumption of specie payments there has also been a marked and gratifying improvement of the public credit. Bonds of the government bearing only four per cent. interest have been sold at or above par, sufficient in amount to pay off all the national debt which was redeemable under the present laws. The amount of interest saved annually by the process of refunding the debt since March 1, 1877 is $14,297,117. The bonds sold were largely in small sums and the number of our citizens now holding public securities is much greater than ever before.

The amount of the national debt which matures within less than two years is $792,121,700, of which $500,000,900 bear interest at the rate of five per cent, and the balance is in bonds bearing 6 per cent. interest. It is believed that this part of the public debt can be refunded by the issue of 6 per cent. bonds, and by the reduction of interest which will thus be effected, about $10,000,000 can be annually saved to the treasury. To secure this important reduction of interest, a plan which it is hoped will be provided by Congress during the present session.


III. GOLD AND SILVER COINAGE.


The coinage of gold by the mints of the United States during the last fiscal year was $78,185,911. The coinage of silver dollars since the passage of the act for that purpose, reported Nov. 1, 1879, was $45,000,550, of which $12,200,344 have been issued from the treasury and are now in circulation and 2,300,506 are still in the possession of the government. The tendency of the proposition for unity of coin before the United States and the principal commercial nations of Europe to effect a standard of gold and silver in the recognized money of the world, leads me to recommend that Congress refrain from new legislation on the general subject. The great revival of trade, internal and foreign, will supply during the coming year its own instructions which may well be awaited before attempting further experimental measures with the coinage.

I would, however, strongly urge upon Congress the importance of authorizing the secretary of the treasury to suspend the coinage of silver dollars upon the present legal ratio. The market value of the silver dollar being uniformly and largely less than the market value of the gold dollar, it is obviously impracticable to maintain them at par with each other if both are coined without limit. If the cheaper coin is forced into circulation, it will, if coined without limit, soon become the sole standard of value, and thus defeat the desired object, which is a currency of both gold and silver which shall be of equivalent value, dollar for dollar, with the universally recognized money of the world.


IV. RETIREMENT OF LEGAL TENDERS.


The retirement from circulation of United States notes with the capacity of legal tender in private contracts is a step to be taken in our progress toward a safe and stable currency which should be accepted as the policy of the government and the interest and security of the people. It is my firm conviction that the issue of legal tender money, money based wholly on the authority and credit of the government, except in extreme emergency, is without warrant in the constitution and in violation of sound financial principles. The issue of United States notes during the late civil war with the capacity of legal tender between private individuals was not authorized except as a means for rescuing the country from imminent peril. The circulation of these notes as paper money for any protracted period of time after the accomplishment of this purpose was not contemplated by the framers of the Law under which they were issued. They anticipated the redemption and withdrawal of the notes at the earliest practicable period consistent with the attainment of the object for which they were provided. The policy of the United States steadily adhered to from the adoption of the constitution has been to avoid the creation of a national debt, and when from necessity in time of war, debts have been created, they have been paid off on return of peace as rapidly as possible. With this view and for this purpose, it is recommended that existing laws for the accumulation of a sinking fund sufficient to extinguish the public debt within a limited period, be maintained. If any change of the objects or rates of taxation is deemed necessary by Congress, it is suggested that experience has shown a duty can be placed on tea and coffee, which will not enhance the price of those articles to the consumer, and which will add several millions of dollars annually to the treasury.


V. MORMONISM.


The continued deliberate violation by a large number of prominent and influential citizens of the Territory of Utah, of the laws of the United States for the prosecution and punishment of polygamy, merits the attention of every department of the government. This Territory has population sufficient to entitle it to admission as a State. This important change would be difficult while the citizens of Utah, in very considerable numbers, uphold a practice which is condemned as crime by the laws of all civilized communities throughout the world. The Law for the suppression of this offense was enacted with unanimity by Congress more than seventeen years ago, but has remained until recently a dead letter in the Territory of Utah because of the peculiar difficulties attending its enforcement. The opinion widely prevailed among citizens of Utah that the law was in contradiction of the constitutional guarantees. The Supreme Court of the United States has held that the law to be within the legislative power of Congress, binding as a rule of action for all who reside within the Territories. There is no longer any reason for delay or hesitation in its enforcement. It should be firmly and effectually executed. If not sufficiently stringent in the provisions, it should be amended and in aid of the purposes in view, reinforced.

The Moors of Barbary and Tripoli distill an ardent spirit from the fruit of the date palm, the Brazilians from the marrow of the sago tree and from pineapples, and even the poor berries that manage to ripen on the banks of the Yukon have to furnish a poison for the inhabitants of Alaska. Pulque, the national drink of Mexico, is derived from a large variety of the aloe plant; the sap of which is collected and fermented in buckskin sloughs into a torpid yellow,ish liquor of most vicious taste. Cheese in fact, is nothing but coagulated milk in a more or less advanced state of decay. Sauerkraut is cabbage in the first stage of fermentation, which when completed yields quass, the above mentioned Russian tonic. Chicha, a whitish liquid which in Peru is handed around, like coffee after meals, is prepared from maize or Indian corn, moistened and fermented by mastication.

coat is out at the elbows, back up
against the fence; if you have no
hat, you will never become bald.

but when—you will be prouder of
your good nature in the dark
days of adversity, my son, than you
can be of all the honors and all the
fame and position that prosperity
and success can bring you. Never
worry, son; don't fret; it will early
make your face thin and your hair
turn gray.—Bardett. — To Iss'd

He has the courage of simple truth,

The trials that he must bear.
The peril, the ghost that frights him most,
He faces boldly, and like ghost

It vanishes in air.
As wild fowl take by river and lake,

The sunshine and the rain,
With cheerful constant hardihood
He meets the bad luck and the good,

The pleasure and the pain.
Come friends in need, with heart and deed

He gives himself to them,
He has the grace which reverence lends
Reverence, the growing flower that bends

The upright lily-stem.

Though deep and strong his sense of wrong,
Fiery his blood and young,
His spirit is gentle, his heart is great,
He is swift to pardon and slow to hate;

And master of his tongue.
Fond of his sports! No merrier lads

Sweet laughter ever rang!
But he is so generous and so frank
His widest wit or maddest prank

Can never cause pang.
He loves all things that please.
He loves like any boy;
But fosters prudent fortitude;
Nor will he squander fortune good

To buy fleeting joy.
Face brown, fair? little care,

Whatever the hue may be,
Or whether his eyes are dark or light;
If his tongue be true and his honor bright,

He is still the boy for me.
Where does he dwell? cannot tell;

Nor do I know his name;
Or poor or rich? don't mind which;
Or learning Latin, or digging ditch;

I love him all the same.
With high, brave heart perform your part,

Be noble and kind as he,
Then, some fair morning when you pass,
Fresh from glad dreams, before your glass,

His likeness you may see.
You are puzzled! What, you think there is not

A boy like him—surmise
That he is only bright ideal?
But you have power to make him real,

And clothe him to our eyes,
You have rightly guessed: in each pure breast

Is his abiding-place.
Then let your own true life portray
His beauty, and blossom day by day

With something of his grace.

But why they should want to erect a monument to Adam way out in the southern tier of York State passes our comprehension. FROM AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT OF THE BOSTON. Oct. 4.—When a State of such size as Massachusetts has SIX conventions preliminary to one election, you may truthfully say it has a good deal of politics to the fore. We have already had five of our conventions, and the regular Democrats have called the sixth. Will this be the last? The women-suffragists are not usually backward about assembling in convention, but hear that some of them think it wise to refrain from further special agitation until the experiment of allowing women to vote in school matters has been tried, while others are willing to forego a convention on the ground that Wendell Phillips tells the truth when he says that General Butler is enthusiastically at the head of the woman's rights movement. The liquor dealers and extreme Anti-Prohibitionists have sometimes thought it needful to emphasize their position by holding a convention, but this year most of them appear ready to accept General Butler as their candidate without the formality of a special nomination. Hence we indulge the hope that this convention ends the business for 1879.

The finger of Fate does not yet indicate with certainty who is to receive the nomination at Faneuil Hall on the 9th instant. Some of the faithful in the part of the state think it would be wise to put the standard into the hands of the Hon. Reuben Noble this time. He is chairman of the State Central Committee, lives at Westfield, has considerable service in the Legislature, is popular in a certain sturdy way, is a genuine Yankee in every respect, and a citizen of most excellent quality. Down at this end of the State the Hon. Charles Thompson of Gloucester is generally spoken of as the best to lead the forthcoming hope. His late term in the lower branch of Congress gave him a National reputation, and I doubt if the regular Democrats have any more popular man in the State. Here in Boston there is a little talk of again presenting Ex-Governor Gaston, but he is much more devoted to law than to politics at present, and I know no reason for supposing he would take the nomination. The names of two or three other gentlemen have been mentioned in this connection, but no one of them has anything more than a merely local following or strength.

There can be little question that the strongest possible nomination for the Republicans would be that of Mr. Thompson. That is, he would hold more of the Democrats from going to Butler than any else can. But I am told by one of the delegates to the coming convention, a gentleman who believes in Thompson and would like to see him nominated, that he says he will not take the nomination, and that he will declare in a letter to be made public at the convention, should the movement in his behalf become strong as to render its success probable. When asked the why and wherefore of this reluctance on Thompson's part, I was answered that very likely he had no notion of running for Congress again next year. In which case I can see that he might not want to antagonize any part of the Democratic vote of his district by taking a prominent part in the fight of this year.

The nominee of last year is the unknown quantity of to-day. Of course Judge Abbott is against General Butler as decidedly now as he was then. He says quite openly that he does not wish to be put forward again as the candidate of the party. But there are Democrats, men who voted for him last year, who assert that this declaration is at variance with his action, and especially at variance with both the words and actions of a considerable number of his friends, men of mature years who have heretofore been accustomed to rule in the party councils. The gentlemen who question the sincerity of the Judge's declaration, say that he is in training for the New-England position in the Cabinet of the Democratic President to be chosen at the next National election, and that he and his confidants are of the opinion that the exigencies of the situation renders it advisable for him to undergo the martyrdom of another defeat. How much there is in all this will probably be revealed next week.

The talk of the street and the clubs is that the Butler party would prefer the nomination of Judge Abbott, and are ready to further his chances by all the means in their power, not because they have any belief of helping him to command a winning position in 1880, but because they regard him as the weakest of those who prominently mentioned as possible candidates. With all his acknowledged abilities Judge Abbott is a cold politician.

They can and that if this battle is to be won, the old man must take the field in person. Otherwise he might well shut up shop and withdraw from his candidacy at once. Of course he will blunder before the campaign ends, but he had better afford to do that than keep silent.

The notion that appears to prevail in some outside quarters that Mr. Long is not generally acceptable to the great body of the Republicans in the State is one that should speedily be abandoned by all who wish to get a true sense of the situation here. Mr. Long is a thoroughly capable man in every respect. Most of those who favored another rally on him to advantage; dignity clothes him as with a garment; he and "Charley" Thompson—merely to mention the names by which they are commonly called—shows the availability of either gentleman as a candidate for a year when every vote is needed.

General Butler will yet get the better of his adversaries, that is my prediction. Almost to a man, they are said to favor him still—lunt this year, and may well have justified their opinion. And it is the solemn and sober truth that General Butler is about the only man in the Butler party in this end of the State about whom there is any juiciness whatever.

Speakers enough here are among his followers, heads of one sort or another, quite ready to run hither and yon and recite their prosy essays about the necessity of reform; but not one of them seems to have the least idea that he is the chastest argument against the reform he breaches. AFTER THE FUNERAL SERVICE.

Wesemann, an undertaker at No. 265 Atlantic
avenue, Brooklyn, was examined by Justice Walsh,
of that city, yesterday. On Thursday last Charles
Elein died at his residence No. 473 Baltic street,
and his family engaged Wesemann to inter the re-
mains in the family plot in Evergreens Cemetery,
East New York. Wesemann informed that the
family were in straitened circumstances and
could not pay more than $50 on account and the re-
mainder of the bill by instruments. The under-
taker agreed to the conditions. The time for hold-
ing the services then set for Friday afternoon,
and at the time appointed the house was filled
with friends of the deceased. At the conclusion of the
services Wesemann refused to proceed with the
funeral arrangements until the balance of his bill
was paid. The family promised that they would
make every exertion to get the money immediately
after the burial. Wesemann turned a deaf ear to their
entreaties and abruptly left the house, where the
utmost confusion prevailed. Son of the
Secretary La Fetra, of the Board of Health,
who at once despatched a messenger for Wesemann
with the notice that he must report at the office
of the Board forthwith. The undertaker appeared
late in the afternoon and in explanation of his
conduct said he had not been paid for his services.

"Why, the son says that you accepted $50 in ad-
vance and agreed to receive the balance in install-
ments," said the Secretary.

"I will not leave until I get it," replied the undertaker.

"The body must be buried," said the Secretary,
"and the Board can compel you to bury it."

Secretary La Fetra then read aloud the following
section of the Sanitary Code:—

Sec. 70. The disposal of a dead body shall
be subject to the Board of Health President
thereof.

A demand for the permit then made by the
Secretary, but Wesemann refused to deliver it up,
saying that no Board of Health could compel him to.
Wesemann then left, after being informed by
the Secretary that he would be allowed just twenty
minutes to return the permit. Shortly after young
Elein again called upon the Secretary and said
that Wesemann had removed his father's body from the
coffin and taken the latter and other things from
the house, remarking, with a laugh, that he guessed
he had them now. Mr. La Fetra entered a com-
plaint against Wesemann and a warrant for his
arrest issued. The Commissioners of Charities
were then appealed to and the remains were de-
cently interred in the family plot under their
supervision. Wesemann arrested and taken before
Justice Walsh yesterday morning, as above stated.
He pleaded not guilty, but held for examination
in the sum of $500. The family of the deceased
are very respectable people.

Incoming communication has been received at the British War Office from Lord Chelmsford: I regret to have to report a very disastrous engagement on the 23rd day of January, between the Zulus and portion of No. 4 column, which was left to guard the camp, about ten miles in front of Rorke's Drift. CHESTER, PA.

In the early part of last week, the pleasure yacht Zulu, owned by Mr. Murray of Media, Pa., was robbed by some unknown parties of stun vessels.

Elsewhere in this paper will you find
an advertisement for Special Election
to be held on Saturday, the 14th inst,
to vote on the question whether an
amount not to exceed $5,000 shall be
added to the already burdensome indebt-
edness of the incorporated village of
Woodsfield.

The bonded debt of this Corporation
is already $7,700. Owing to the hard
times and scarcity of money there has
been no levy made to meet any part of
this indebtedness, except the interest for
more than three years past.

As money matters have not yet improved to any appreciable extent, is it a
wise financial policy to impose an addi-
tional tax and debt of $5,000, as propos-
ed by the Council, bearing 7 per cent in-
terest, for the purpose of grading and
paving our streets?

We, with other Taxpayers, are of
opinion that it is not. It is suggested
in lieu of the plan advocated by the
Council, that that body levy the last cent
possible, under the law, and apply the
amount, about $5,000 each year, to paving
the streets, and by so doing save $3.50
per annum in the way of interest. In
six years time $30,400 would be levied
paid out, and applied on our streets, and
the saving in the way of interest to that
time on the sum proposed to be issued
by the Council in bonds would be $1,100,
which would make the net cost of
the whole only $500. Now let us see
what the Council plan will cost at the
end of six years.

Bonds, $5,000
Interest, 8 years at 7 per cent, $1,100
Total, $6,100

At the end of six years our indebted
ness and interest will foot up as fol-
lows:

Present indebtedness, $7,700
Int. 6 yrs at 7 per cent, about $400

Proposed indebtedness, $5,000
Interest for 6 years, $1,100

Total, $13,500

And by the time these bonds are pre-
sented for redemption the taxpayers of
the Corporation will have paid over $40,600, of which sum over $1,000 can be
counted as interest.

This picture is not a lovely one when
viewed by those who have the bills in
foot. Another very important matter
to be considered by voters is the fact
that when the railroad is completed in
this place, and we all expect that it will
be before the 1st of January next, men
who contemplate coming here to build
and to go into business, will be likely to
hesitate, and perhaps give up coming
when informed that the debt of the Cor-
poration, in the proposed sum is voted
to be $13,700 and that they will be heavily
taxed to clear it up.

Consider carefully, taxpayers, before
you vote to impose grievous burdens
upon those who are barely able to meet
present taxation, and at the same time
contract an indebtedness that will hang
over all who pay taxes for at least ten
years to come, and in the end will prove
more damaging to the town, in the way
of preventing improvements, than any
other one act you can possibly perform.

to Washington, and for nearly two years
life was to him but a long summer's day
of happiness. Never was husband loved
more faithfully or trustingly than he by
her; never wife more tenderly and af-
fectionately than she by him. In Jan-
uary, 1847, his wife died, leaving an
infant child, the daughter who has since
grown up to be the head of his house-
hold and of her husband's. At the time
of her death there was no railroad con-
necting the capital with the West. The
fond husband would not think for a
moment of consigning the remains of
the one he loved and held most dear to
a grave amid strangers, and so he deci-
ded to transport them to Chillicothe for
burial. He procured the services of an
undertaker and started with them, he
riding behind on horseback. When
night would overtake them they would
stop at the nearest hotel, and he would
have the coffin taken from the hearse
and borne to his own apartment, where
he kept watch over it until morning
came and time to start again. More
than a week elapsed in this mournful
trip, yet at no moment during that time
was his mournful gaze taken from the
last remains of her whom he had loved
so dearly in life and could scarce part
with in death. After her burial he re-
turned to Washington and finished his
term of office, and then betook himself
with his child to the home at which he
has just died.
The prominence which Mr. Allen had
achieved in the politics of the nation and
by this time to raise personal opposi-
tion to him, headed by the partisans of
various corrupt schemes which he had
opposed. The mere fact of his refusal to
accept constructive mileage was in itself
an unpleasant rebuke to the current
virtue of public men. With those acting
with these motives was a knot of young
and ambitious men headed by G. L.
Vallandigham, who formed a successful
combination to oust Mr. Allen from his
active leadership of the party. It is no
unworthy of note that the next great
success enjoyed by the party in Ohio
came quarter of a century later, with
William Allen as candidate for Governor. The estrangement which there
sprang up between Mr. Allen and some
of the leaders of the party was first brok-
en when he joined in reception of Mr.
Vallandigham in 1868, and from that
time on he remained in active and un-
tiring sympathy with the chiefs of the
party. In 1873 he was nominated to
Governor and elected by majority over William M. Noyes, the previous
majority by which Governor Noyes was
elected having been 20,168, and Presi-
dent Grant's majority in the previous
year being 27,631. In 1875 Governor
Allen was re-nominated by the Demo-
crats to Governor, his opponent being
Rutherford B. Hayes, the present occu-
pant of the White House. The details
of that contest are matters of too recent
occurrence to need more than mention.
In the St. Louis convention, where Mr.
Tilden was nominated by the Democrats
as their candidate for the Presidency,
Governor Allen's name was presented,
by General Ewing, the present Demo-
cratic candidate for Governor of Ohio.
On the first ballot Ohio gave him her
votes, West Virginia 10, and Missouri
more, making 56 in all. There were only
two ballots, but on the second ballot
Governor Allen's friends contributed
only 4 votes—those from Missouri.
Governor Tilden's, Ohio's and West
Virginia's still voting solidly for him,
whom General Ewing had called a
"Farmer Statesman."
A correspondent who left on a long visit
to Governor Allen and in whom the venerable gentleman told the
story of his life, thus described him, "He
is still a stout, robust man. In
mind, his clear blue eyes have lost
none of their wonderful magnetism and
his sonorous voice but little of its old
time volume. His tall frame has been
somewhat under the weight of passing
years but, like the old stone dwelling
place he loves so well—a house which
sheltered a Governor of Ohio fifty years
ago—he as yet gives no indication that
he will not be able to withstand the
blasts of many winters to come." The
correspondent asked the apparently strong
old man why he did not enter public life
again and after a long pause received
this for a reply:
"Because I am one of the few old
men who, unlike Henry Clay, know
when we have reached our highest point
and when it is time for me to give up
power which I am no longer strong
enough to use for the good of the peo-
ple."
The character and the record of Gov-
ernor Allen were summarized in this
editorial column of the World, which
said of him in July, 1873, just before
the election as Governor:
Mr. Allen has never had any partic-
ipation in the politics of the country ex-
cept as a stanch, zealous and unwaver-
ing patriot of the best and purest sort.
It is the good fortune of Mr. Allen
that he have had no connection with the Fug-
itive Slave act, no hand in the repeal
of the Missouri Compromise, no complic-
ity in the attempts to thrust slavery on.

From the Richmond Dispatch.

MAY 10, 1879.

A regular session of East Hanover Presbytery was held at the Second Presbyterian church, in this city, Saturday night. Mr. J. N. Rose, of Portsmouth, acting as moderator. The business of Presbytery was laid under its care. Mr. B. A. Pendleton of Richmond, as candidate for the ministry. Mr. Pendleton is a student of Richmond College. His name was examined by Rev. Dr. Witherspoon, and after a careful examination as to his views in seeking the ministry, he was received under the care of the Presbytery and committed to the oversight of a Committee of Education. The Presbytery then adjourned.

At St. John's Presbyterian church, a large congregation attended the installation of Rev. S. H. Foster of that church. The sermon was delivered by Rev. Dr. Thomas L. Preston of Richmond, and was an exceedingly good and appropriate one. Rev. J. N. Rose returned the charge to the pastor, and Rev. Walters pronounced the charge to the people. At the conclusion of the services the ring of worship was given to the pastor.

The funeral of Mrs. Mary J., wife of A. E. Roper, took place from the Baptist church this afternoon. She died during the evening of consumption, after a long and painful illness. Deceased was daughter of Mr. J. W. Pace, of Danville. She was a lady of accomplishment and of beauty of character.

Rev. Dr. W. W. Bennett preached at the First Street Methodist Episcopal church this morning and night. In the morning, presented to the congregation the funds of Randolph Macon College and received a contribution of $500.

A mass-meeting of the congregation of Wesley Methodist Episcopal chapel was held yesterday afternoon to consider the question of changing the site of their church. A motion was made to donate a site at a more central location on Halifax street, which was accepted by the meeting, and it was determined to erect a church edifice upon it at a cost of $1,000. The work will be commenced at an early day. Rev. R. N. Chandler is the pastor of this church, and the building is too small to accommodate the growing congregation.

In the list of licenses issued by the commissioner of the revenue in this city for the fiscal year commencing Nov. 1, 1879, there are 81 to commission merchants, 20 to attorneys at law, 9 to physicians, 5 to dentists, 3 to land agents, and 50 to insurance companies, represented by seven agencies.

The regular monthly meeting of the Methodist Sunday-School Association was held at the Church in Blandford yesterday afternoon. The organization of the Association was reported to be 154 officers, teachers, and scholars, with an average attendance of 115. An interesting fact was reported to the meeting from the Episcopal school—that during the recent revival there twenty-three of the scholars were converted, and had since joined the church, making twenty-three additions to the church within a few weeks.

Rev. Dr. Gibson, Rev. Dr. Harris, Rev. Thomas Spencer, Rev. E. B. Cooke, and Rev. George G. Sutton, rectors of the Episcopal churches in this city, will leave to-morrow afternoon for Fredericksburg to attend the Council of St. Paul's and Grace churches. By reason of having assistant rectors, will each be entitled to two delegates in the Council.

Miss Mattie B., daughter of Mr. H. B. Spiers, residing on Halifax street, died suddenly yesterday morning at the residence of her grandmother, Mrs. Leonard, in Prince George county, where she was on a brief visit. She was in the sixteenth year of her age, and her family here were not even aware that she had been sick. Her mother is residing in another section of this State. ROBIN ADAIR.

Thomas Check was arrested at Jack-
town, Penn, for setting fire to Beth-
any College last month, on Friday
night by Deputy Sheriff Curtis and
taken to Wellsburg Saturday morning.
On the way the people, who had suffer-
ed from the frequent incendiarisms
recently, turned out and threatened to
lynch Check, so the sheriff was compel-
led to remove the prisoner to Wheel-
ing, W. Va., for safety. Dr. Parkinson,
prominent dentist, of Wellsburg,
W. Va., was also arrested as accessory.

In Todd county Minnesota, few
days ago, the house in which John and
Michael Moede lived was burned, and
John charged that a neighbor named
Coldall did it because he had induced
Coldall's wife to leave her husband and
live with him. Suddenly Coldall and
man living with him were missing, and
in the house signs of foul play were
found. John Moede was arrested on
suspicion and lodged in Long Prairie
Jail. On Saturday, becoming frighten-
ed at the threats of the crowd from the
surrounding country, he confessed that
he had helped his brother to mur-
der the two men and bury the bodies. Dur-
ing the night Moede was taken from
the Jail by a mob and hanged. Michael
Moede was arrested Sunday at Lax
Henry and taken to Long Prairie, where
the mob waits to serve him the same
as his brother.

The revision of the Bible, now near-
ly completed, has been a very expensive
work. There are fifty-two members of
the committee, and these meet for five
days in every three weeks. No salar-
y is paid to any one of them, but they are
allowed their travelling and inn ex-
penses. These, with other items, will
bring the cost of the first edition of the
Revised Bible, as estimated by the Uni-
versity Press Company, which is re-
sponsible for it, to about 100,000, and
consequently it has been determined to
sell the first few copies at high price.
The new Bible will receive no "author-
ization" either from Parliament or con-
vocation. It has been discovered in-
cidentally during the sittings of the com-
mittee that the so-called authorized
version never was in fact authorized
either enthusiastically or politically. It
made its way by its own merits, and the
revised Bible is expected to do the
same.

AN ARREST OF JUDGMENT GRANTED


BROOKLYN, Sept. 20, 1879.


The trial of Wilhelm Buchholz for the murder of Johann Heinrich Schultz brought to fitting conclusion yesterday noon by verdict of murder in the first degree. Thus ends one of the most remarkable and dramatic murder trials in the annals of criminal justice, and one which has a series of startling surprises and unexpected developments. There is no doubt that but for the State's Attorney's persistent determination to hold Buchholz and to ferret out the truth from the only human being who was with the murdered man on the night of the murder it would still be mystery, and Buchholz would probably have carried out his intention of going to Australia and there enjoyed the fruits of his crime. Next to the State's Attorney who first fixed upon Buchholz the guilty person, the chief credit of the successful issue of the case belongs to Mr. Pickering and that arch detective Ernst Stark, who, while performing disagreeable, perilous duty with marvellous cleverness, showed yet in the trial that detective could still be a gentleman of perfect modesty and dignity and a truthful witness, for even the counsel for the defendant admitted that his integrity and veracity.


All night long the court room was open, and it was not until nearly four o'clock this morning that Buchholz retired and the court room became deserted. But the multitude of curiosity seekers thronged back to the court room early in the morning. Young girls entered with suffering from the want of sleep, to which they had voluntarily subjected themselves to be present at the announcement of the verdict. Buchholz looked somewhat pale, but he had steeled himself in wonderful manner for the ordeal he was about to undergo. A sort of continued his role of the previous evening with the same success, issuing and chatting humorously outwardly at ease—perfectly indifferent as to his fate. The general impression which his demeanor created was that he had buoyed himself up to a confident anticipation of disagreement of the jury expectation in which he was confirmed by his bevy of charming friends.


THE JURY BE DISCHARGED.


At nine o'clock whisper ran round. The jury's fearful silence came over the audience, and many eyes turned wistfully at the prisoner to see how he would react. Disappointment ensued when it was found that the jury had only come in to announce that they could not agree. The court could not comply with this request however and said that the interests of justice and of the State urgently required their handing in a verdict; if they now discharged the case it would have to be tried again exactly as it had been. The same facts, the same arguments precisely, would be employed, and His Honor could not see why this jury not capable of coming to just and righteous conclusion upon these facts and arguments the next jury that might be empanelled. He would therefore be compelled to send them back for further consideration of the case, and would urge them, in view of the kind of verdict they could do so consistently with their oaths.


One of the Jurors said that there was some misapprehension among the jury as to the precise meaning of the law which required the evidence of two credible witnesses or its equivalent for conviction, and also to the various degrees of murder which the law would warrant.


The Judge instructed the jury that every material circumstance need not be testified to by two witnesses but that the conviction must rest upon the evidence of at least two witnesses, which the jury might consider its equivalent.


The jury then retired and at noon returned again. The court room was now packed. A beautiful basket of flowers and grapes had been presented to the prisoner and several paper bags of confectionery, pastry, &c. lay also on the seat beside him. The foreman of the jury, a white haired solemn looking old man, looked sternly at Buchholz.


THE VERDICT PRONOUNCED.


The clerk said in loud, ringing voice, "The State against Wilhelm Buchholz. Gentlemen of the jury please answer to your names as they are called. As you answer please RISE."


The roll was called, and after the jury had all risen the clerk continued, "Gentlemen of the jury, have you agreed upon a verdict?"


The Foreman (in low tone)—"We have."


The Clerk (solemnly)—"Buchholz, stand up. Look upon the foreman. Foreman, look upon the prisoner. What say you? Is the prisoner guilty or not guilty of the crime whereof he stands indicted?"


The foreman replied looking straight into Buchholz's eyes:—"Guilty of murder in the first degree."


At this announcement there was just the faintest change in Buchholz's face, but his whole strength seemed to fail, he dropped into his seat buried his face in his hands and moaned and sobbed with apparent agony.


The Clerk—"Listen to your verdict as it stands accepted by the Court and is ordered to be recorded. You upon your oaths do say that the prisoner, Wilhelm Buchholz, is guilty of murder in the first degree, and so you say."


The foreman bowed assent, and after the counsel of Buchholz had given notice of motion in arrest of Judgment for a trial the court adjourned. The motion in arrest of Judgment will be argued next Saturday week and on that day, if it is overruled, Buchholz will receive sentence of DEATH. He never uttered a word on being taken back to Jail.

LONDON, July 12.—They buried Prince Louis Napoleon this morning at Chislehurst and the evening papers contain full accounts of the ceremony. There are, however, one or two points which I wish to say a word. First as to the Queen of England's share in the business. Her Majesty has seen fit to be present on this occasion. I presume she would say—I know that it is said for her by those who seek to defend her act—that she went in order to show her personal sympathy with the bereaved mother. Nothing can be urged against sentiment of that kind. The Queen's attachment to the Bonapartes, the hereditary enemies of her house, dates from the exchange of visits between herself and Prince Albert on one side, and the Emperor and Empress on the other, in 1855, or whereabouts. The diary which she has herself given to the world through Mr. Theodore Martin is explicit on that point. Her liking for the Emperor and affection for his wife was never dynastic, and ceased to be—if it ever was—purely political after that date; though it was long the cue of one section of English society to represent the intimacy between them as contracted in the public interest. Ever since the collapse of the French Empire the Queen of England has openly and repeatedly given proofs of the sincerity of her friendship for the deposed occupants of the French throne. Since the death of the Emperor, her sympathy with the Empress grew, naturally enough, still closer. The two women had another tie in common—that which bound each to the memory of her dead husband. If kings are mortal, queens are also human, and womanly. In so far as Queen Victoria's presence at Chislehurst to-day is a declaration of her continuing love for the ex-Empress, and of sorrow for the fresh calamity which has befallen her, there is, I repeat, just criticism to be made on it.

But a queen is queen first and a woman afterward. That is one of the penalties she pays for her exalted station. No professions of private regard can absolve her from public duties, strip her demonstration of to-day of its public character. She cannot lay off and put on her royal character at will. France will know that the Majesty of Great Britain was present at the burial of a pretender to the French throne. It is certain, that to the French mind, the Queen's presence will seem like a manifestation of political goodwill to the house of Bonaparte, and hence of political illwill to the Republic. The inference may be erroneous, but it will be drawn, and it will intensify the hostility to England which for some time past has been steadily gaining ground among the French. This is what the Queen ought to have taken into account. This is above all what her Ministers ought to have pressed upon her. Her visit to Chislehurst is an act of State—nothing less. Her purpose must have been known to her advisers. They were bound to bring her attention to the consequences of it, and she bound to give heed to their representations and whether these representations conformed to her private judgment or private inclinations or not, to abide by them. Their constitutional duty and hers were equally plain. Nobody knows, or can know, whether Lord Beaconsfield and his colleagues acted in this. It's better to suppose that they neglected their duty than that the Queen disregarded the counsel which she would have been bound to follow if offered to her.

The opinion of most classes, have lately shown themselves singularly indifferent to the political consequences of their emotional indulgences. They have been for weeks past on the brink of serious quarrel with France. Their conduct with respect to Egypt and to Greece, which has not been emotional but selfish, has done much to alleviate French friendship. Their conduct about the Prince has done even more. The fuss made about him when he set out on his journey to South Africa was trivial compared to what has since occurred, but it provoked an indignation none the less dangerous because for the most part suppressed. You heard the mutterings of it in private if you happened to be in Paris. If there was less of it in the papers, it is because the serious journals of Paris are capable of great prudence in treating delicate international questions. Whether this sentiment of prudence will get the better of the very different feeling sure to be stirred by this deplorable escapade of the Queen, we shall know in a day or two. In either case the English public may be trusted to preserve its usual stodgyness in the matter. Subject as Englishmen are to odd explosions of feeling, they are the last people in the world to perceive that others may have sensibilities as well as themselves. They wrap themselves up in the conviction that where no offence is meant none will be taken.

It cannot be hoped that the French understand the extent to which the Queen's acts are dictated by caprice, but the French are too little in the habit of following the course of events in foreign countries with sustained attention. Few of them have minute knowledge of what goes on in the royal family of England. They may not be aware how far the Queen's observance of conventionalities depends on her state of health or mood at the moment. Possibly they never heard that she quitted Windsor for the north two days before the arrival of the Emperor of Russia some years ago, or that she left the residence when the Empress of Germany was her guest two days before her guest's departure, hurrying off this time also to Balmoral. To put it in a homely way, her Majesty does very much what she feels like doing. She is sorry for the mother of the dead boy, and went to Chislehurst this morning to tell her so, and to offer her what comfort she might in the midst of her distress. She did not mind offending the Emperor of Russia her own son's father-in-law, nor the Empress of Germany to whose son her eldest daughter is married. And she minds quite as little wounding the just susceptibilities of a friendly nation who have not yet learned to distinguish between the individual and the constitutional acts of a constitutional sovereign. In the present case, the offence is not lessened by the fact that not only the Queen but nearly the whole royal family were in attendance on this Bonapartist coffin. The Prince and Princess of Wales, the Dukes of Edinburgh and Connaught and Prince Leopold all went. A brief statement of facts existing
at the commencement of the war is
necessary to proper understanding of
the position occupied by the loyal ele-
ments of East Tennessee at that time,
and, also, to show the motives that in-
spired their action in remaining loyal
to the Federal Government during the
war.

In the Presidential contest of 1860,
the Whig party of Tennessee support-
ed Bell and Everett, and their battle-
cry was, "The Union, the Consti-
tution and the enforcement of the laws."

Its adherents held that the United
States was a nation; that the National
Government was created by the people
and not by the States; that sovereignty resided alone in the people, and not
in the State governments; that the
people, the fountain and head of all
sovereignty, had delegated certain su-
preme powers to the National Govern-
ment, and among them the power to
coerce any State into obedience to
those powers.

On the other hand the advocates of
"States-rights," disunion Democracy
of Tennessee, and the South
claimed and proclaimed that the
United States was a mere confedera-
tion of sovereign States, and that all
powers not expressly delegated to the
central government were reserved to
the different States—and consequently
it was optional with any state to
sever her connection with, and peace-
ably to secede from the rest whenever
in her judgment, it was her interest
to do so.

In the year 1860, Mr. Lincoln was
elected President, and his election
compelled the Southern Democracy to attempt to
carry out their ideas and principles.
The Southern States, one after another
went through the farce of seceding
from the Union. Secession was a
Democratic measure throughout.
Every State that seceded from the
Union was Democratic; every State
that seceded had a Democratic Governor
at the time, and every secession
ordinance passed was adopted by a
Democratic Legislature.

Under the lead and teaching of
Judge Nelson, Judge Trewhitt, Horace
Maynard, W. G. Brownlow, and many
others less prominent, the body of the
Whig party of East Tennessee in their
adherence to principle, remained al-
firm, as steadfast, and as immovable
as were their native hills and moun-

the Western divisions of Tennessee
the large mass of the Whig party
finally went into and sympathized
with the rebellion.

BURNETT STATION, June 16

About 2 O'Clock P. M. Last Saturday, this town was struck by one of the most terrible wind, rain and hail storms ever witnessed by any one in its destructive course. About half past one O'Clock there was noticed in the south-west a heavy, black and ominous looking cloud, and when it approached the scene it was indescribably grand and one never he foresighted by those who were unfortunate enough to have witnessed it. The cloud was one

GRAND PANORAMIC SCENE.

Heaven's artillery kept up one continuous roar. Suddenly peals would burst forth which would fairly shake the earth, then in a few moments would come vivid, blinding flashes of lightning, dashing athwart the sky in its zigzag course, and ever and anon striking the earth with a loud report. Rain fell in perfect torrents, and hills of prodigious ice covered the ground to the depth of two inches.

Immense corn fields, which few days ago we're pleasure to look upon, are now bare in the street. To look at the hedges reminds one of mid winter; they bring completely stripped of their green and tender foliage. Immense damage was done in the direction of Shawnee Mound, the wind playing havoc with the large wheat field in that section.

The large store occupied by J. J. Lee, 25x60 feet, was moved fifteen feet from its foundation, and left in such condition as to render it a total loss. A new dwelling house east of the store, 19x26 feet, was blown over and completely demolished, parts of which have been found a quarter of a mile from the foundation. Fortunately this dwelling had recently been vacated.

Passing on to the northeast, the hurricane next struck the residence of Mr. Levi Helfry, capsizing it and literally tearing it to pieces, and fatally injuring a little girl, 5 years of age, by

FRACTURING HER SKULL.

Dr. J. F. Robinson was immediately called, and in short time took out several pieces of bone which had penetrated the skull. It is thought she cannot possibly recover.

Passing on two miles further to the northeast, the storm passed in the direction of Windsor. In that place one house was blown down and a child badly hurt. Further than this point your correspondent has not learnt of any damage being done, though it may have continued for miles.

Losses BY THE STORM.

J. J. Lee's loss is about 5000. Samuel Logan told your correspondent that his loss would foot up to 8,100. S. Wherry, who is proprietor of the town, will lose 500. M. Helfry's property loss is fully $500. J. J. Lee's large barn on his farm west of town was moved seven feet from its foundation. J. C. Bryson's smoke house was blown down. Dan Nash's workshop, house and barn were all moved and more or less damaged.

Miles and miles of fencing were blown down. The damage between Shawnee Mound and Windsor it is estimated will amount to 5000.

INCIDENTS

Quite a number of people were at the store when the storm struck, among whom were John Braden, Bud Draper, Dave and Joe Bryson and old Mr. Baker. The latter while the storm was raging with all its fury, stepped out and attempted to cross the street, when he was taken in charge by the wind and hurled in an instant to the ground. While in this prostrate condition he received considerable damage from the hail, which was falling thick and fast.

John Braden was blown across the road and through a hedge fence into Mr. Nehr's field.

Bud Draper was carried about forty rod and lodged in a hedge.

J. Braden was hurled against a wagon wheel and comfortably bruised.

Horrible Murder.

Last Monday cold blooded murder was committed against Miller from Lebanon, which for atrocity and guilt and deliberation has never been eclipsed by any deed of brutality ever enacted in this country. Mr. Geo. W. Miser was mowing in his field in company with his younger brother. A sudden crack of a rifle was heard in the woods adjoining the field. Mr. Miser clasped his hands to his breast and cried out "Oh, Lord!" and fell down in the furrow dead. Who it was that did the deed is not known to the public. Miser farm is in the valley of Goodwin Hollow. The murder took place between three and four O'Clock in the evening. It is said that the Miser's life had been threatened. A pistol was found in his pocket when he was dead.

The affair has roused the people here.

right direction was slow. There were many
circumstances against it from those who
dreaded the hardships it entailed, too much to
have any adequate conception of the substan-
tial advantages that would accrue from it. A
resa nostra was compounded but when it
was found that Grant was inflexible in his hos-
tility to every form of quackery, the idea of
legislative tinkering was reluctantly aban-
doned.


At the subsequent session—nine months later
the resumption act was passed. It was a
mosaic. It had in it features of attraction to
the inflationists by which it gained their votes,
and enough of the hard-money men counte-
nanced it to secure its enactment. It was not
satisfactory as a whole to either. But the sem-
sible and practical mind of the President saw
in it the promise of resumption at a future
day. For that reason he signed it, it certain-
ly had all the appearance of preparing the way
for unlimited expansion. It authorized the
creation of as many banks as capitalists chose
to organize, and for as much currency as they
wished to issue. There was no restriction up
on the amount. But the law worked a great
deal better than it was meant to. There was
so little demand for paper money that there
was very small chance of profit from increas-
ing the supply. Contraction followed—very
moderately it is true, but every dollar with-
drawn was a benefit to the people. The infia-
tionists were disappointed and tried to defeat
the part of the scheme that decreed the ulti-
mate restoration of specie payments. The
Democratic party, with that strange fatality
which for thirty years has always led it to take
the wrong side of every public question, placed
its Presidential candidates on an anti resump-
tion platform in 1876. Happily they were de-
feated. Efforts to repeal the act have been
thwarted, and now we are just beginning to en-
joy the benefits which have at last rewarded
the patience and fortitude with which five
years of continual tribulation and financial
disorder have been borne. In the cheerful
faces of the multitude who encounter each day
in the marts of traffic and upon the streets
of the city one can readily discern the evil
evanescence of renewed confidence and hopefulness.
The feeling is almost universal that the cou-
ntry is at the threshold of a grand and prosper-
ous career; that enterprise will have free
course; that capital relieved of the distrust
which is inseparable from a deprecated and
fluctuating currency, will be poured into all
the channels that invite it with assurances of
safety and remuneration; and that the indus-
tries of the land will be quickened into new
life and vigor, promoting individual thrift and
augmenting the national wealth.


YARMOUTH.
